What exactly does a $12 trillion "accumulated trade deficit" mean?

The simple answer is, over that amount of time, the US imported more goods than it exported, and either paid out, or accumulated debt from manufacturers and traders in other countries, in that amount. (Some of the debt was likely lost to them via bankruptcy, etc; the same is true in the opposite directions too.) In effect, we paid $12 trillion out to them that hasn't re-entered the country through trade. So what happened to that money?

A majority of it was brought back into the US as investment rather than trade. Buying stock in US companies, real estate, other forms of investment. A bit of it was brought in by people emigrating to the US, letting them establish themselves here. The remainder, a few trillion dollars, is still outstanding, mostly fungible instruments like US government and corporate bonds. That remainder is a great leverage the US has against a trade deficit; the money is just sitting there, acting as a temptation to spend here in the US.

Protective tariffs placed by the US will tend to reduce imports, as the things people buy get more expensive. They unfortunately also usually result in retaliatory tariffs from other countries, which also reduces US exports. So placing protective tariffs tends to be a zero-sum game. You could argue that we should do the same thing other countries do, subsidizing industry in order to employ people and generate a trade advantage; but subsidies have a lot of other problems, including enabling corruption and increasing the power and scope of government.

Using tariffs may also assist in paying off the huge amount of debt the government has racked up; of course this will only help if the government stops running a deficit.
